query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In multilayer protective coatings made from high‐entropy alloys, the engineered alternating layers with deliberately mismatched lattice parameters and interfacial morphologies create robust barriers that impede dislocation nucleation and motion by generating localized interfacial strain fields, thereby reducing time-dependent plastic deformation compared to homogeneous coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high‐entropy alloy film or coating with a uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Fabrication of multilayer coatings by alternating high‐entropy alloy layers with different compositions or lattice parameters designed to establish controlled, mismatched interfaces with non‐planar morphology.
generation.conditions: High temperature and stress conditions that induce creep (dislocation-mediated deformation), with identical thermal cycling and mechanical loading applied to both multilayer and homogeneous (control) samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Engineered multilayer interfaces featuring a modest negative lattice misfit and serrated interlayer boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The deliberate lattice misfit and non‐planar interface morphology produce localized strain fields that pin dislocations and hinder their climb and glide, thereby slowing the creep rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under comparable high-temperature, high-stress conditions, the multilayer coatings will exhibit a significantly lower steady-state creep strain rate and more uniform strain distribution (observed via lower local strain concentrations) relative to homogeneous coatings.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous high‐entropy alloy coatings that lack engineered interfacial mismatches and hence do not benefit from additional dislocation barrier effects.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for service conditions where creep deformation is dominated by dislocation motion and where the multilayer interfaces remain chemically and structurally stable; it may not apply if temperatures are so high as to cause phase transformations or interfacial degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise range of lattice misfit and interfacial morphologies required to optimize the creep resistance, as well as the quantitative improvement in creep rate, remain to be fully determined for different high‐entropy alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one set with the engineered multilayer architecture (featuring alternating high‐entropy alloy layers designed to produce controlled lattice misfit and serrated interfaces) and a control set consisting of a homogeneous high‐entropy alloy coating prepared under identical overall compositional conditions. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature creep testing under controlled stress conditions.
measurements: Steady-state creep strain rate via creep tests
Local dislocation density and distribution using transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Interface morphology and strain distribution via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep strain rate or show no evidence of reduced dislocation mobility/accumulation compared to the homogeneous coatings under equivalent testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As shown in Figure 13, all creep curves exhibit the typical three-stage behavior. Notably, the duration of the steady-state creep stage decreases with increasing |δ|. The relationship between creep life and |δ| is non-monotonic. Specifically, within the range of −0.1688% to −0.084%, creep life increases as |δ| increases. Conversely, within the range of −0.8075% to −0.1688%, creep life decreases as |δ| increases. The longest creep life is observed at δ = −0.1688%. To gain further insight into the underlying mechanisms, atomic strain distributions were analyzed, as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14a,b compare atomic strain maps of HESAs with negative (−0.1402%) and positive (0.1402%) lattice misfits. At t = 130 ps, the model with the negative lattice misfit (Figure 14a) exhibits lower atomic strain, suggesting enhanced resistance to deformation. This implies that a negative lattice misfit stabilizes the γ′ phase, strengthens the γ/γ′ interface, and impedes dislocation motion, thereby improving creep resistance. A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility.
